No. 24-1287 

-------------------- 

In the 

Supreme Court of the United States 

-------------------- 

Learning Resources, Inc., et al., 

Petitioners,

v. 

Donald J. Trump, President of the United States, in his official capacity, et al. 

-------------------- 

ON PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI BEFORE JUDGMENT
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA CIRCUIT

-------------------- 

REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO EXPEDITE CONSIDERATION OF 
THE PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI BEFORE JUDGMENT 

-------------------- 

The IEEPA tariffs affect every American and countless American businesses.  

Despite  having  been  held  unlawful  by  the  two  courts  that  have  addressed  their 

legality, the IEEPA tariffs continue to cost Americans billions each day, sow financial 

uncertainty throughout the country, and reshape the Nation’s economy.  This Court 

has granted certiorari before judgment nearly twenty times since 2019, including in 

cases  of  similarly  “staggering”  legal,  economic,  and  political  significance.    Biden  v. 

Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477, 489, 502 (2023); Sup. Ct. R. 11.  The consequences are too 

great to justify the government’s unwarranted plea for delay. 

1

1.    Respondents  do  not  dispute  that  this  case  is  one  of  imperative  public 

importance that only this Court will ultimately resolve.  Nor do they dispute that the 

President  has  asserted  unfettered  tariffing  power  under  IEEPA;  that  no  other 

President in the statute’s nearly 50-year history has ever claimed any authority to 

impose tariffs; that the IEEPA tariffs equate to the largest peacetime tax increase in 

U.S. history; or that they are pushing small businesses to the brink of bankruptcy 

and pose an “existential threat” to Petitioners.  Pet. App. 37a. 

Given the IEEPA tariffs’ unprecedented nature and monumental impact, it is 

difficult to imagine a case more likely destined for this Court’s docket.  Respondents 

do  not  say  otherwise.    They  do  not  contend,  for  instance,  that  a  decision  from  the 

courts of appeals will extinguish the need for this Court’s review.  On the contrary, 

Respondents raise the prospect of this Court granting review “either before or after 

the D.C. Circuit has issued its judgment,” including over the summer, after more time 

and resources have been wasted—just not now.  Resp. 6-7.     

Respondents  also  hint  (in  passing)  that  certiorari  before  judgment  is 

inappropriate  because  Petitioners  prevailed  below.    Resp.  3.    But  the  lower  court 

injunctions  have  been  stayed,  and  Petitioners—like  thousands  of  other  American 

businesses—are  continuing  to  suffer  irreparable  harm  on  an  extraordinary  scale.  

Two terms ago, the government found itself in a similar position—prevailing in the 

district court but stymied pending appeal—in a case affecting many fewer Americans 

but  similarly  involving  hundreds  of  billions  of  dollars  and  ongoing  financial 

uncertainty.  Despite being the prevailing party, the Solicitor General sought a writ 

2

of certiorari before judgment, and this Court granted it.  See Nebraska, 600 U.S. at 

489.  Nothing prevents this Court from following that same course here.  Pet. 31-32. 

2.  Not only is this case undeniably important, it should be decided now.  The 

economic  consequences  of  the  billions  in  IEEPA  tariffs  that  American  businesses 

(and, ultimately, American consumers) pay each day are mounting.  Just this week, 

a popular home goods chain that sources most of its merchandise from China cited 

the IEEPA tariffs as a reason it entered chapter 11 bankruptcy.1  As the district court 

found,  Petitioners  are  experiencing  “massive  disruptions  in  [their]  supply  chain, 

business relations, and business operations” and are bracing for a dramatic decline 

in sales.  Pet. App. 38a.  They have sharply curtailed importation from China, their 

primary  source  of  manufacturing.    Id.  at  55a.    Meanwhile,  business  planning  has 

become a “nightmare” for Petitioners and other American companies, which cannot 

know  what  IEEPA  tariff  the  President  might  impose  next  week  or  the  week  after 

that,  and  will  not  know  whether  the  tariffs  are  here  to  stay  until  this  Court 

definitively resolves the matter.2

Respondents’ response to these escalating harms is a feeble one:  They suggest 

Petitioners  can  obtain  refunds  if  the  IEEPA  tariffs  are  ultimately  held  unlawful.  

Resp. 3-4.  But that misses a critical point:  businesses cannot receive refunds for all 

the goods they are unable to import in the first place due to prohibitively high tariff 

1 Jodi Xu Klein & Connor Hart, Retailer At Home Files Chapter 11 Bankruptcy, Hobbled by 
Tariffs and Debt, WALL ST. J. (June 16, 2025), https://www.wsj.com/articles/at-home-retailer-chapter-
11-bankruptcy-ad3b6e01?st=vDvx4A&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink. 

2  Ben  Berkowitz,  The  only  trade  certainty  is  uncertainty,  AXIOS  (June  13,  2025), 

https://www.axios.com/2025/06/13/trump-tariffs-uncertainty. 

3

rates.  Nor can they “recover the value of the *** sales, business opportunities, market 

share, or customer goodwill” consequently lost.  Pet. App. 39a.  And, of course, refunds 

do little good to a bankrupt business. 

Respondents nonetheless argue it should be enough that the D.C. Circuit and 

Federal Circuit (in the parallel CIT cases) will proceed on expedited schedules.  See 

Resp. 6-7.  But just this week, rejecting Petitioners’ request to align timing with the 

Federal Circuit’s, the D.C. Circuit issued a schedule that does not complete briefing 

until  August  8—seven  weeks  from  now—and  that  did  not  set  a  date  for  argument 

(presumably leaving it to after the summer recess).  Order, Learning Resources, Inc. 

v. Trump, No. 25-5202 (D.C. Cir. June 18, 2025).  On that timeline, the D.C. Circuit 

will not issue a decision for months.   

Respondents observe that Petitioners can seek certiorari before judgment if the 

Federal Circuit moves more quickly (as it almost certainly now will).  Resp. 6.  But if 

forgoing a decision from the D.C. Circuit is fine then, why not now?  Wasting that 

court’s resources with briefing and argument (without decision) helps no one.  To the 

extent  this  Court  prefers  hearing  this  case  in  tandem  with  the CIT  cases,  there  is 

every  reason  to  think  the  CIT  plaintiffs  will  immediately  seek  certiorari  before 

judgment if this Court grants here—or this Court can adjust the schedule should the 

Federal Circuit issue a decision in early August (before D.C. Circuit briefing is even 

complete). 

Respondents’ entreaty for the normal 30 days to respond to the petition is hard 

to take seriously.  Having filed a response to Petitioners’ motion within 24 hours, and 

4

having  filed  emergency  application  after  application  in  both  this  Court  and  others 

(including  in  the  tariff  cases  when  they  lost  in  the  district  court  and  CIT), 

Respondents are clearly able to respond quickly.  Petitioners’ proposed schedule is no 

faster than timelines typical of the emergency docket.  In any case, this Court can 

determine whatever prompt schedule makes most sense in light of the pressing need 

for  timely  resolution  and  the  Solicitor  General’s  suggestion  that  this  Court  can 

consider a petition for certiorari after the start of summer recess.  See Resp. 7. 

3.  Shifting to cert-opposition mode, Respondents argue that jurisdiction does 

not in fact lie in the federal district courts.  See Resp. 4-6.  But whether the federal 

district  court  had  jurisdiction  rises  and  falls  with  the  principal  merits  question—

whether  IEEPA  is  a  law  that  provides  for  tariffs—and  is  the  central  question  this 

Court  will  consider  if  it  grants  certiorari.    Mot.  8-9;  Pet.  30-31;  see  28  U.S.C. 

§ 1581(i)(1) (CIT has exclusive jurisdiction over “any civil action *** that arises out 

of any law *** providing for *** tariffs”); Brownback v. King, 592 U.S. 209, 217 (2021) 

(where “the merits and jurisdiction *** come intertwined[] *** a court can decide all 

of  the  merits  issues  in  resolving  a  jurisdictional  question,  or  vice  versa”  (internal 

quotation marks and ellipsis omitted)).  This case thus is a proper vehicle to resolve 

“both the jurisdictional issue” under Section 1581(i) “and the merits.”  K Mart Corp. 

v. Cartier, Inc., 485 U.S. 176, 182 (1988) (holding jurisdiction proper in district court).      

Respondents suggest that even if IEEPA is not a law that provides for tariffs, 

jurisdiction still lies exclusively in the CIT because the President’s executive orders 

modified the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (“HTSUS”) and such 

5

modification is a statutory provision of law.  Resp. 5.  But that is not the jurisdictional 

theory adopted by the CIT.  See V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v. United States, --- F. Supp. 

3d ---, No. 25-00066, 2025 WL 1514124, at *8 (Ct. Int’l Trade May 28, 2025).  And it 

is not the theory adopted by two district courts that transferred their cases to the CIT 

on the ground that IEEPA did provide for tariffs.  See Emily Ley Paper, Inc. v. Trump, 

No.  3:25-cv-464-TKW-ZCB,  2025  WL  1482771,  at  *4-6  (N.D.  Fla.  May  20,  2025);

Webber  v.  United  States  Dep’t  of  Homeland  Sec.,  No.  25-cv-26-GF-DLC,  2025  WL 

1207587,  at  *4-6  (D.  Mont.  Apr.  25,  2025).    Respondents  have  cycled  through 

(meritless) jurisdictional theory after theory in search of a justification for taking this 

case out of federal district court. 

In any case, Respondents’ latest jurisdictional theory is wrong.  Congress gave 

the CIT exclusive jurisdiction only over actions “that arise[] out of” a law providing 

for tariffs.  28 U.S.C. § 1581(i)(1) (emphasis added).  As the district court recognized, 

Pet.  App.  18a,  the  “substantive  law”  that  gives  rise  to  each  of  Plaintiffs’  claims  is 

IEEPA, making this “a[] civil action” that “arises out of” IEEPA, not the HTSUS.  See 

International  Lab.  Rights  Fund  v.  Bush,  357  F.  Supp.  2d  204,  208  (D.D.C.  2004) 

(analyzing  CIT  jurisdiction  based  on  “substantive  law  giving  rise  to  [plaintiffs’] 

claims”). 

*** 

This  Court  should  order  an  immediate  response  to  the  petition  from  the 

Solicitor General, expedite consideration of that petition, and then grant it, so that 

the lawfulness of the IEEPA tariffs can be resolved as early as possible next Term.   

6

Respectfully submitted, 

Pratik A. Shah 
   Counsel of Record 
AKIN GUMP STRAUSS HAUER

& FELD LLP 

2001 K Street NW 
Washington, DC 20006 
pshah@akingump.com 

Counsel for Petitioners 

June 20, 2025 

7

RULE 29.6 STATEMENT 

Petitioners Learning Resources, Inc. and hand2mind, Inc. are private, family-

owned corporations.  Learning Resources, Inc. and hand2mind, Inc. have no parent 

corporation  or  publicly  held  corporation  that  owns  10%  or  more  of  either  entity’s 

stock. 

8

CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE 

Pursuant to Rules 29.3 and 29.5 of the Rules of this Court, I certify that all 

parties required to be served have been served.  On June 20, 2025, I caused a copy of 

the foregoing Reply in Support of Motion to Expedite Consideration of the Petition 

for a Writ of Certiorari Before Judgment to be served by email and overnight delivery 

on the below-named counsel for Respondents: 

Daniel Winik 
Bradley Hinshelwood 
Michael S. Raab  
U.S. Department of Justice 
(DOJ) Civil Division, Appellate Staff 
950 Pennsylvania Avenue, NW 
Washington, DC 20530 
Tel: 202-514-2000 
daniel.l.winik@usdoj.gov 
bradley.a.hinshelwood@usdoj.gov 
michael.raab@usdoj.gov 

D. John Sauer 
Solicitor General of the United States 
Department of Justice 
950 Pennsylvania Ave., NW, Room 5616 
Washington, DC 20530-0001 
Tel: 202-514-2203 
SupremeCTBriefs@USDOJ.gov 

June 20, 2025 

Pratik A. Shah 
Counsel of Record 

9
